value_chain_position: Surgical-robotics platform and implant maker - sells the robot and instrumentation into every spine-surgery deployment, the toll-taker of the surgical-robotics layer
cost_curve_verified: Proxy versus company-reported: DISAGREE, and the proxy is wrong. The deterministic gross-margin proxy in the input bundle reads 'compressing', down 6.8 percentage points over three years, but it anchors on fiscal 2022's 74.2% - the pre-merger standalone Globus margin - so it is measuring the NuVasive revenue mix, not an operating trend. The filings and the company agree in the other direction: gross margin was 69.2% in the first quarter of 2026 against 67.3% a year earlier, and 67.4% for full-year 2025 against 58.9% in 2024, with management claiming a sixth consecutive quarter of adjusted gross-margin expansion on the 24 February 2026 call. Use the reported figures.
gm_trajectory: Expanding margin on growing revenue - the good combination. Gross margin 69.2% in the first quarter of 2026 on revenue up 27% year on year, versus 67.3% on a 0.8% constant-currency decline a year earlier; 67.4% for full-year 2025 on revenue up 16.7%, versus 58.9% in 2024. That is pricing power and vertical integration (95% of production is United States based), not volume bought with price.
bull_thesis:
The case is that the market is still pricing Globus Medical as a low-growth orthopaedic implant company while it has quietly become the fastest-growing share-taker in spine, with a fortress balance sheet and a margin structure that is still improving.

Start with what is verifiable. United States spine revenue grew 2%, 5.7%, 9.6%, 10% and 10% across the five quarters from the first quarter of 2025 to the first quarter of 2026 - an acceleration, not a fade - against a market that chief executive Keith Pfeil put at '3%, give or take' on 7 May 2026. Fifty-eight consecutive weeks of United States spine implant growth is a falsifiable disclosure; a company inventing momentum does not volunteer a counter that breaks in public the first week it stops being true. Gross margin expanded 850 basis points in 2025 and a further 190 basis points year on year in the first quarter of 2026. Base-business adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation - roughly operating cash profit) reached 33.4% for 2025 and 35.7% in the fourth quarter, hitting the mid-30s target management set publicly at the time of the 2023 NuVasive merger, on the schedule it promised. Roughly $900 million of merger debt is gone, the final $450 million repaid in the first quarter of 2025, and the company now carries about $515 million of net cash.

The valuation is the argument. On trailing twelve-month figures to 31 March 2026 - revenue of $3.10 billion, EBITDA of $880 million, free cash flow of $600 million - the shares change hands at 11.9 times enterprise value to EBITDA and yield 5.5% on free cash flow. The comparable set: Intuitive Surgical at 28.1 times, Stryker at 22.5 times, Medtronic at 14.0 times, Zimmer Biomet at 11.6 times, Smith+Nephew at 9.6 times. Globus sits in the Zimmer Biomet neighbourhood while growing several times faster, earning a higher return on invested capital (9.7% and rising, against Zimmer Biomet's 5.3%), and carrying net cash where Zimmer Biomet carries 3.2 times leverage. On earnings the gap is starker: $81.06 against management's raised 2026 adjusted earnings guidance of $4.70 to $4.80 is 17.1 times, against roughly 20 times for Smith+Nephew, 23 for Medtronic, 24 for Zimmer Biomet and 35 for Stryker.

The misunderstood item is the robot line. Enabling Technologies revenue fell 31% and 27% in the first and third quarters of 2025, and the market read that as losing the robotics war. Management's own explanation, given consistently from November 2025 onward, is that it is deliberately converting outright capital sales into operating leases and rentals to place more systems faster, accepting lower upfront revenue recognition in exchange for implant pull-through. If that is true, the reported decline in a line worth about 4.5% of revenue is a chosen accounting outcome and the economics are showing up exactly where they should - in the 10% United States spine implant growth. Cumulative robotic procedures went from over 100,000 in the first quarter of 2025 to almost 130,000 a year later, and the fourth quarter of 2025 delivered record Enabling Technologies revenue of $55.6 million, up 18.5%, made up 'primarily cash deals with immediate revenue recognition' - which is the pipeline that was said to be merely delayed, arriving.

Conditions the bull case requires: United States spine holds at or near double-digit growth as the NuVasive cross-sell tailwind laps; adjusted gross margin stays above 68%; Nevro stabilises somewhere near a $350 million annual run rate rather than continuing to shrink; and the board either restarts the buyback at a sensible price or leaves the $515 million of net cash alone. If those hold, the parts are worth around $119 per share.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that this is a bad business. It is that the durable, high-margin part of it is a spine implant company in a market growing 3% a year, that the exciting part is being commoditised in front of us, and that the people running it have already told us - with their own chequebook - that they think the stock is worth more than it is.

Begin with the buyback, because it is the cleanest evidence of judgement available. Management confirmed on 7 May 2026 that it has repurchased over 10 million shares for more than $600 million at an average price of $160. The stock is $81.06. That is roughly $300 million - over $2 per share - destroyed on timing. And the pattern is worse than the average: $190 million spent in the first quarter of 2025 and $300 million across 2025, then nothing at all in the first quarter of 2026 while the company issued $26 million of stock through option exercises. They bought heavily near the highs and stopped near the lows. Insiders have made zero open-market purchases against 23 sales totalling 239,178 shares.

Now the order book, or rather its absence. There is no disclosed backlog figure, no book-to-bill ratio and no installed-system count anywhere in five quarters of calls, despite analysts asking in every one of them. What management offers instead is a cumulative procedure counter - a number that can only go up - and adjectives: 'the deal pipeline is robust', 'we did not lose any pipeline deals to competition'. Undated, unquantified pipeline language is worth nothing. The one substantive thing management did disclose, in November 2025, is the tell: 'hospitals are requiring surgeons to go through the review of all the offerings that are out there... that has kind of elongated some of the deals.' That is a description of a premium capital sale turning into a commodity bake-off. Medtronic announced United States clearance of its Stealth AXiS robotic spine platform on 13 February 2026 - planning software, navigation and robotic assistance in a modular design built for both hospitals and ambulatory surgery centres - and claims a spine-technology installed base ten times its nearest competitor's. Three months later Globus told investors on 7 May 2026 that 'no other competitive systems, including recently introduced products, have been able to replicate' its robot. That is promoter language, unsupported, about a competitor that had just cleared a next-generation system. Stryker's Mako and Zimmer Biomet's Rosa are in the same fight. The lease pivot is best read not as strategy but as the price of staying in the room.

Three numbers price the downside.
First, the mechanical deceleration. Nevro entered the revenue base in April 2025, so reported growth of 27% in the first quarter of 2026 becomes high-single-digit growth from the second quarter onward by pure arithmetic - management's own 2026 guidance is 8.2% to 9.6%. Screens and momentum funds that bought a 27% grower will be looking at a 9% grower by the 6 August print.
Second, Nevro itself. The contribution fell from roughly $99.7 million in the fourth quarter of 2025 to roughly $82.7 million in the first quarter of 2026, management has declined to guide it for four consecutive calls, and its own chief executive warned of continued 'choppiness'. The $141.5 million of tax losses acquired with it are worth far less than they sound: management said they flow through over 'a range of 40 to 50 years' as cash-tax savings and give no earnings accretion at all.
Third, input costs and margin quality. Management asserts tariffs are immaterial because 95% of production is United States based, and nine months of margin data have not contradicted it. But a 200 basis point gross-margin reversal on $3.2 billion of revenue is $64 million of EBITDA - about 7% - worth roughly $6 per share at the base multiple. And part of the recent margin gain is a deferral rather than a structural win: research spending was 4.8% of revenue in the first quarter of 2026, down from 5.5% a year earlier, in the quarter directly after management promised on 24 February 2026 to raise it toward 6%. Restoring that costs about 120 basis points of operating margin, roughly $38 million a year.

Add the working-capital reality - 283 days of inventory and a 331-day cash conversion cycle, so growth consumes cash in instrument sets before it produces any, and quarterly free cash flow swings from $26 million to $219 million - plus two unresolved shareholder-law-firm investigations into 'potential self-dealing' opened on 1 June and 16 and 28 July 2026 that name no transaction and cannot be checked against a proxy this review could not retrieve. If the chain turns - hospital capital budgets freeze, the robot becomes a giveaway, spine reimbursement compresses as procedures migrate to ambulatory surgery centres, and Globus re-rates to the cheapest comparable in its group on a lower profit base - the parts are worth about $60 per share. The shares traded at $52.68 within the past 52 weeks, so that is not a theoretical level.
sop_bull:
Favourable sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately): about $119 per share.

The reported segment disclosure in the input bundle is stale - it splits fiscal 2024 into Spine of $2.37 billion and Emerging Technology of $154 million, which predates the Nevro acquisition. The parts below are rebuilt from the company's own quarterly base-business and Nevro splits and its stated Enabling Technologies revenue, for the twelve months to 31 March 2026: core musculoskeletal (spine implants, trauma and neurosurgical) about $2.58 billion; Enabling Technologies (ExcelsiusGPS robots, imaging, navigation, service) about $140 million; Nevro interventional pain about $377 million. Total $3.10 billion, which ties to reported revenue.

Parts:
1. Core musculoskeletal implants - assumes 2026 guidance is delivered and margin keeps expanding, giving roughly $900 million of segment EBITDA. Valued at 16 times, between Medtronic at 14.0 and Stryker at 22.5, credited for double-digit United States spine growth against a 3% market and a mid-30s adjusted margin: $14,400 million.
2. Enabling Technologies - about $150 million of revenue at 5 times sales, crediting the installed base of nearly 130,000 cumulative procedures, the recurring service and disposable annuity behind it, and the fact that the lease conversion understates the reported line: $750 million.
3. Nevro interventional pain - about $380 million of revenue at 1.5 times sales, on a business whose adjusted margin has already gone from breakeven to 16.2% and whose cash flow turned positive within two quarters of ownership: $570 million.
4. Acquired tax losses - $141.5 million of cash-tax savings released over 40 to 50 years, discounted hard: $40 million.
5. Net cash - $515 million today, building toward roughly $700 million over the horizon on $600 million of annual free cash flow: $700 million.

Total equity value $16,460 million over 138.2 million diluted shares = $119 per share. Sanity check: that is 25 times the midpoint of management's raised 2026 adjusted earnings guidance, below Stryker at 35 times and Zimmer Biomet at 24.5 with far better growth, and $2 above the highest published street target of $117.
sop_bear:
Adverse sum-of-the-parts, assuming the chain regime turns against it: about $60 per share.

The adverse world is specific: hospital capital budgets tighten further, the robot finishes its journey from premium product to giveaway as Medtronic's Stealth AXiS (cleared 13 February 2026), Stryker's Mako and Zimmer Biomet's Rosa fight for the same operating rooms, spine reimbursement compresses as procedures migrate to ambulatory surgery centres, the promised step-up in research spending finally lands, and Nevro keeps shrinking.

Parts:
1. Core musculoskeletal implants - United States spine decays from 10% toward the 3% market rate as the NuVasive cross-sell laps; adjusted margin gives back roughly 300 basis points between the research step-up (about 120 basis points, or $38 million a year) and a 200 basis point gross-margin reversal from input costs, tariffs and currency (about $64 million). Segment EBITDA falls to about $720 million. Valued at 10 times - below Zimmer Biomet's 11.6 and near Smith+Nephew's 9.6, the cheapest in the peer group: $7,200 million.
2. Enabling Technologies - about $140 million of revenue at 2 times sales, treating it as a shrinking, competitively eroded capital line rather than a platform: $280 million.
3. Nevro interventional pain - written back to the $250 million all-cash purchase price paid in April 2025, which is 0.66 times its current revenue. Justified by four consecutive refusals to guide the business and a contribution that fell from roughly $99.7 million to roughly $82.7 million between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026: $250 million.
4. Acquired tax losses - nil. They are only worth something against taxable income that this case does not produce at the assumed rate: $0.
5. Net cash - $515 million as it stands on the 31 March 2026 balance sheet ($630 million of cash and short-term investments against $115 million of debt including finance leases). No cash build is credited, and the risk that it is spent on another full-price acquisition is real given the board's demonstrated price judgement: $515 million.

Total equity value $8,245 million over 138.2 million diluted shares = $60 per share. That is 12.6 times the midpoint of 2026 adjusted earnings guidance and 26% below the current price. It is not a stretch: the shares traded at $52.68 within the past 52 weeks.

risk_reward: Stated as levels, not ratios. Against $81.06 on 4 August 2026: the adverse case marks the shares at $60, the base case at $94 and the favourable case at $119. The 52-week range is $52.68 to $101.40; the 50-day average is $79.72 and the 200-day average is $83.94, so the stock is currently trading through its longer-term average. There is no structural floor: no deal terms, no tender, no announced asset sale, and net cash of about $3.73 per share is far too small to act as one. The $60 adverse level is a valuation floor built from a de-rate to the cheapest comparable in the peer group on a 12% lower profit base, not a hard backstop.
catalyst_status_note: The nearest dated, company-confirmed event is second-quarter 2026 results, scheduled for after the New York close on Thursday 6 August 2026 - two days from now - announced in a company press release dated 16 July 2026. What that print tests is also dated: on 7 May 2026 management reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $3.18 to $3.22 billion and raised adjusted diluted earnings-per-share guidance to $4.70-$4.80 from $4.40-$4.50. No contractual payout, no deal terms and no binding third-party obligation attaches to it - it is a scheduled disclosure event, nothing more. Recorded for the file only: in this lane a live event is neither a reason to buy nor a reason to discount, and the case here rests entirely on the residual gap between price and the parts value.
peer_comps_note:
Measured against the assigned competitor set on trailing twelve-month figures as of 4 August 2026 (enterprise value to EBITDA, enterprise value to sales, return on invested capital, free cash flow yield):
- Globus Medical: 11.9 times, 3.38 times, 9.7%, 5.5%
- Intuitive Surgical: 28.1 times, 11.5 times, 15.1%, 2.5%
- Stryker: 22.5 times, 5.44 times, 9.8%, 3.6%
- Medtronic: 14.0 times, 3.75 times, 6.1%, 4.9%
- Zimmer Biomet: 11.6 times, 3.04 times, 5.3%, 9.9%
- Smith+Nephew: 9.6 times, 2.45 times, 9.1%, 6.7%

The picture is unambiguous: Globus is priced in the Zimmer Biomet and Smith+Nephew bracket - the low-growth orthopaedic implant bracket - while earning a return on invested capital ahead of both and nearly level with Stryker's, growing its core United States business at roughly three times the market rate, and carrying net cash where Zimmer Biomet carries 3.2 times leverage and Smith+Nephew 1.7 times. Intuitive Surgical's 28 times is the multiple a genuine robotics monopoly earns, and this analysis deliberately does not apply any part of it to Globus, because management's own repositioning of the robot from premium product to placement channel forfeits that claim. The base-case 13.5 times applied to the core implant business is therefore roughly a Medtronic multiple - a mature-medtech multiple for a business with better growth - which is the conservative way to frame the gap. Two caveats: Globus's cash conversion cycle of 331 days is the worst in the group and structurally so, given field instrument sets; and its ratio of goodwill and intangibles to total assets, at 40%, is lower than Zimmer Biomet's 64% or Medtronic's 57%, meaning less acquired-asset risk sitting on the balance sheet.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market, and where we disagree with the bulls.

The street's central error is a categorisation error. Analysts are valuing Globus Medical as a low-growth orthopaedic implant maker - 11.9 times enterprise value to EBITDA, essentially Zimmer Biomet's 11.6 - while the business is compounding faster than anything else in that bracket. Its United States spine line has grown 9.6%, 10% and 10% in the last three reported quarters against a market management sizes at 3%, its gross margin has expanded 850 basis points in a year, and it hit the mid-30s operating-cash-margin target it set publicly in 2023 on the exact schedule promised. The comparable multiple for that profile is Medtronic's 14 times at minimum, and arguably higher.

The specific assumption that is factually wrong is the reading of the robot line. The consensus narrative treats Enabling Technologies revenue falling 31% in the first quarter of 2025 and 27% in the third as evidence Globus is losing the robotics fight to Medtronic and Stryker. But the line is only about 4.5% of revenue, and management has stated repeatedly, from 6 November 2025 onward, that it is deliberately converting outright capital sales into operating leases and rentals: 'you might be moving units but not seeing the same sales dollars if you're trying to look at this apples-to-apples' (24 February 2026). The evidence supports that. The fourth quarter of 2025 delivered record Enabling Technologies revenue of $55.6 million, up 18.5%, made up 'primarily cash deals with immediate revenue recognition' - the supposedly lost pipeline arriving - and cumulative robotic procedures went from over 100,000 to almost 130,000 across the year. The economics land in implant pull-through, which is precisely where the 10% growth is appearing. A shrinking reported number caused by a deliberate change in how revenue is recognised is not demand destruction, and the market is pricing it as though it were.

The second, quieter street error is on earnings quality, and it runs the other way. Reported 2025 earnings per share of $3.92 is inflated - the second quarter of 2025 carried $203 million of net income on only $76 million of operating income, helped by roughly $112 million of other income and a negative tax charge, being the accounting effects of the Nevro purchase and a valuation-allowance release. Clean reported earnings were nearer $3.15. Any screen or model anchored on $3.92, including the $188 'Buffett' fair value carried in this system's own input bundle, is anchored on a number that will not repeat. Management's adjusted $3.98 for 2025 and its $4.70-$4.80 guide for 2026 are the honest handles, and at $81.06 that is 17.1 times a figure growing about 19%.

Where we disagree with the bulls: the $115 and $117 published targets require a robotics-platform multiple that management's own language has forfeited. When the chief executive describes the Excelsius suite as 'the execution layer' whose purpose is 'driving capital placement... that enable implant sales growth', he is telling you the robot is a channel cost, not a profit pool. Intuitive Surgical's 28 times belongs to a company that sells the system and the disposables into a market it created. Globus is fighting Medtronic's Stealth AXiS, cleared 13 February 2026, and Medtronic claims a spine installed base ten times its nearest competitor's. The reconciled fair value of $94 deliberately gives the robot line no platform premium at all.

Finally, the street itself is drifting the wrong way at the margin: price targets averaged $100.71 over the past year, $98.88 over the past quarter and $94.20 over the past month, with UBS at $82 on 28 July 2026 and Stifel at $80 on 8 July sitting against Singh at $115 on 13 July. That spread - $80 to $117 on the same company in the same three weeks - is itself the signal: nobody on the sell side is confident, which is usually a better setup than unanimity.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain no solvency risk whatsoever and one large, entirely mechanical optical risk. There is no debt maturity wall - roughly $900 million of merger debt was extinguished by the first quarter of 2025 and only $115 million of debt-like obligations remain against $630 million of cash and short-term investments. There is no cash burn: trailing free cash flow is $600 million on $3.10 billion of revenue. The balance sheet cannot be the accident here.

What can go wrong is this:

First and largest, the growth optics collapse by arithmetic. Nevro entered the revenue base in April 2025. From the second-quarter 2026 print - due after the close on 6 August 2026, two days from now - the acquisition is fully lapped, and reported revenue growth falls from 27% to the 8.2%-9.6% management itself guided for the full year. Nothing will have deteriorated, but every momentum screen and quantitative growth filter that bought a 27% grower will be looking at a 9% grower within 48 hours. That is the most likely source of a drawdown between here and year-end, and it is entirely predictable.

Second, Nevro is still deteriorating on the top line. Its contribution fell from roughly $99.7 million in the fourth quarter of 2025 to roughly $82.7 million in the first quarter of 2026, and management has now declined to guide it on four consecutive calls while warning of continued 'choppiness' and 'lumpiness'. Another step down of that size takes roughly $70 million out of the annual run rate, enough to push consolidated growth toward the bottom of the guided range and force the question of whether the guide holds.

Third, the quarterly cash line is violently lumpy and will look worse than it is. Free cash flow by quarter over the past five: $136 million, $26 million, $219 million, $192 million, $163 million. The $26 million quarter - the second quarter of 2025 - was the direct comparable to the one about to be reported, and was caused by $86 million of cash taxes paid plus set-building. With 283 days of inventory and a 331-day cash conversion cycle, growth in this business consumes cash in instrument trays before it produces any. A soft cash quarter is seasonal, but it will be read as a break.

Fourth, the enabling-technology line is seasonally weakest in the first half and is being actively converted to leases, so a soft print there is close to guaranteed - the first quarter of 2026 came in at $26.9 million against $55.6 million in the fourth quarter of 2025. Management flagged the sequential step-down in advance, but a second consecutive soft quarter will revive the 'losing to Medtronic' narrative regardless of cause.

Fifth, input costs. Commodities are a cost line here, never a revenue line: titanium, cobalt-chrome and polymer feedstock, plus tariffs and currency, all hit gross margin. Management has asserted since 8 May 2025 that the exposure is minimal because '95% of our production is U.S. based', and nine months of expanding margin have not contradicted it - but the sensitivity is worth naming: a 200 basis point gross-margin reversal on $3.2 billion of revenue is $64 million of EBITDA, about 7% of the total, worth roughly $6 per share at the base multiple. A third-party observer flagged currency and inflation pressure on 22 June 2026.

Sixth, the governance overhang. Two shareholder law firms opened investigations - Purcell & Lefkowitz on 1 June 2026 into directors' duties 'in connection with recent corporate actions', and Kuehn Law on 16 and 28 July 2026 into 'potential self-dealing'. Neither release names a transaction, a date or a party; these solicitations are routine and frequently amount to nothing. But the company's proxy statement filed 24 April 2026 could not be retrieved for this review, so the underlying facts are unverified in either direction. It is an open question, not a finding, and it is exactly the sort of question that becomes a headline at an inconvenient moment.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-liquidation setup here, and it is important to be clear about that rather than manufacture one. The company pays no dividend, so there is no yield-focused shareholder base to be flushed out by a cut. There is no lock-up expiry, no convertible overhang, no covenant, no index-deletion risk, and no pending pivot that would breach anyone's mandate. The register is ordinary institutional and index money - Dimensional Fund Advisors at roughly 1.77 million shares, Bank of New York Mellon at roughly 743,000, California State Teachers' Retirement System at roughly 130,000, per first-quarter position filings reported through late July and early August 2026 - and the recent flow in those disclosures is net accumulation, not distribution.

The real positioning risk runs the other way, and it is a momentum unwind rather than a washout. The shares are up roughly 44% over the past year. Over the eight weeks to 16 July 2026 a single research syndicator published five separate pieces branding the name a 'strong value stock', a 'top value stock for the long-term' and a 'strong momentum stock', plus head-to-head comparisons against Medtronic and Penumbra. That is what narrative saturation looks like at the retail-screen layer: the idea is no longer undiscovered, it is a screen staple. The cohort that arrived on the momentum and growth factors during a 27%-reported-growth quarter will be holding a high-single-digit grower from 6 August onward, purely by the lapping arithmetic, and factor rebalances are indifferent to the reason. That is the mechanism most likely to produce the entry level this analysis wants - not distress, just factor rotation out of a name whose headline growth rate is about to halve for reasons that have nothing to do with the business.

One asymmetry worth noting: the company itself is the marginal buyer that is currently absent. It spent $300 million on repurchases across 2025 and precisely nothing in the first quarter of 2026, while issuing $26 million of stock through option exercises. If the board restarts at $75 or below, having bought at an average of $160, the largest and most price-insensitive buyer in the register returns at exactly the moment the momentum cohort is leaving.
forcing_function:
There is no single event that re-rates this company, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The re-rating requires four more quarters of the same evidence. The dated markers that will either supply it or destroy it:

1. Second-quarter 2026 results, after the New York close on Thursday 6 August 2026 (company release, 16 July 2026). The three things that matter: whether United States spine holds double-digit growth for a fourth consecutive quarter and whether the consecutive-weeks counter extends past 58; whether adjusted gross margin holds above 68%; and whether Nevro stabilises above the roughly $83 million it contributed in the first quarter.

2. The full-year 2026 guidance of $3.18-$3.22 billion of revenue and $4.70-$4.80 of adjusted earnings per share, raised on 7 May 2026 from $4.40-$4.50. Confirmed at the third-quarter print in early November 2026 and delivered in February 2027, this becomes a three-year record of setting public targets and hitting them, which is what earns a multiple. Cut, and the thesis is simply wrong.

3. The buyback. This is the most informative single decision available to the board. The company bought over 10 million shares at an average of $160 and stopped entirely in the first quarter of 2026 at around $80. A restart at current levels, funded from $515 million of net cash and $600 million of annual free cash flow, would be the first evidence that the board's price judgement has corrected - and would put the largest price-insensitive buyer back in the market. Continued absence, or worse, another full-price acquisition, is the signal to stay away. Management said in February 2026 it will 'continue to look at share repurchases when the time is right' and will also 'look at tuck-in M&A'.

4. The research step-up. Management committed on 24 February 2026 to raising research spending from about 5% toward 6% of revenue. First-quarter 2026 spending was 4.8%, down from 5.5% a year earlier. Whether that promise is honoured determines how much of the margin expansion is real.

5. The unresolved governance question - the proxy filed 24 April 2026 and the shareholder investigations announced 1 June and 16 and 28 July 2026. Not a catalyst; a risk marker that needs to be closed out before a full-sized position is justified.
moderator_conclusion:
The right call here is to wait, and to be precise about what we are waiting for.

The business is genuinely good and the forensic file is clean where it counts. Globus Medical is taking share in spine at roughly three times the market growth rate, expanding gross margin while it does so - 69.2% in the first quarter of 2026 against 67.3% a year earlier, and 67.4% for 2025 against 58.9% in 2024 - and converting that into $600 million of annual free cash flow with about $515 million of net cash and no debt worth the name. Management set a public three-year target at the 2023 merger and hit it on schedule in the fourth quarter of 2025. The deterministic gross-margin signal in our own input bundle reads 'compressing' and is simply wrong - it anchors on the pre-merger 2022 standalone margin and measures acquisition mix, not operating direction. On the lie-detector test this lane cares about most, expanding margin on growing revenue, this company passes cleanly.

It also fails two of the lane's other three tests, and that is why the answer is not to buy today.

On order-book durability, there is nothing to grade. Five quarters of calls contain no backlog figure, no book-to-bill ratio and no installed-system count, despite analysts asking in every one. What is offered instead is a cumulative procedure counter that can only rise, and adjectives - 'the deal pipeline is robust'. Undated, unquantified pipeline language is worth nothing, and management's own November 2025 admission that 'hospitals are requiring surgeons to go through the review of all the offerings that are out there' describes a premium capital sale becoming a commodity bake-off. Medtronic's Stealth AXiS cleared on 13 February 2026 with a claimed installed base ten times the nearest competitor's; Globus responded on 7 May 2026 that no competitor 'has been able to replicate' its robot, which is promoter language asserted without evidence. The honest reading, which management's own vocabulary now supports, is that the robot has become a channel-access cost rather than a profit pool. That is a rational strategy and it protects the implant business - but it forfeits any claim on a robotics platform multiple, and the reconciled fair value here gives it none.

On capital discipline, the record is poor in the one dimension that matters. The company bought back more than 10 million shares for over $600 million at an average price of $160, against $81.06 today - roughly $300 million, over $2 per share, destroyed on timing. It spent $190 million in a single quarter in early 2025 and then nothing at all in the first quarter of 2026, while issuing $26 million of stock through option exercises. Insiders have bought nothing on the open market against 23 sales. And research spending fell to 4.8% of revenue in the quarter immediately after management promised to raise it toward 6%, meaning some of the margin expansion investors are paying for is a deferral. Capital expenditure discipline itself is fine - 5.7% of revenue, in line with the guided 5% to 6% - so the problem is not overbuilding; it is price judgement.

On the regime, the robotics chain reads neutral, and nothing in this file argues for overriding that. Commodities are an input cost here, not a revenue driver: a 200 basis point gross-margin reversal from metals, tariffs or currency is worth about $64 million of EBITDA and roughly $6 per share, and the order-cancellation path runs through hospital capital budgets, which management has already watched tighten once.

Reconciling the two cases: the favourable parts are worth $119 per share, the adverse parts $60, and the base case lands at $94. Against $81.06, that leaves roughly $13 of upside to fair value and roughly $21 of downside to the adverse case. A 14% discount to intrinsic value is not a margin of safety on a name that has already risen about 44% in a year, sits above its 50-day average, and reports earnings in two days into a print where reported revenue growth mechanically halves from 27% to single digits as the Nevro acquisition laps. Buying immediately in front of that, at a discount too small to absorb a disappointment, is paying full price for someone else's timing risk.

So: watchlist, not entry. The specific level is $70 to $73 - roughly 15 times management's 2026 adjusted earnings guide and about 10.5 times EBITDA, which would open a discount to fair value near 25% and clear a real margin of safety. That is not a fantasy level: the stock printed $76.20 on 8 July 2026 and $52.68 within the past 52 weeks. The most probable route there is the one this analysis expects anyway - a factor rotation out of the name once the headline growth rate halves for purely arithmetic reasons, most likely in the days after the 6 August print or on any soft second-half Nevro or enabling-technology quarter.

Two things would change the answer. A restart of the buyback at these levels, from a board that bought at $160 and has been absent since, would be the strongest possible signal that the largest price-insensitive buyer thinks the same thing this analysis does - that would justify entering into strength. Conversely, a cut to the 2026 guide, a fifth consecutive refusal to quantify Nevro, or any substantiation of the unresolved self-dealing investigations would move this from wait to pass. On pure value - business quality against the parts value, ignoring timing entirely - this is a four; the single thing withholding a five is that the discount is not yet wide enough. On execution today, it is a three: right company, wrong price, wrong week.
